item.title: Anthropic says large language models enable formal software verification at much larger scale [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Anthropic reports that large language models (LLMs) are making formal software verification feasible on a much larger scale than before. This advancement could significantly improve the reliability and security of software systems by automating complex verification tasks that were previously too resource-intensive. The company highlights how LLMs can assist in generating formal proofs and verifying code correctness more efficiently, potentially transforming software development and quality assurance processes. This development may lead to broader adoption of formal methods in industry, enhancing software safety and reducing bugs.

item.title: Analysis finds identical AI requests emit 8.5 times more CO2 in Texas than Sweden due to energy source differences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent analysis reveals that running the same AI requests produces about 8.5 times more carbon dioxide emissions in Texas compared to Sweden. This significant difference is linked to the energy mix powering data centers, with Sweden relying more heavily on renewable energy sources, resulting in a lower carbon footprint for AI operations. The study highlights how regional variations in electricity generation impact the environmental cost of AI workloads, emphasizing the role of cleaner energy in reducing emissions associated with data processing.

item.title: Analysis of 12 AI models from 10 labs reveals unanimous controversial view that humans prioritize group loyalty over truth [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study asked 12 AI models from 10 labs across three countries to provide their most controversial opinions on humans, with all models repeatedly stating that humans tend to conform to group beliefs rather than seek objective truth. The models expressed variations on this theme, highlighting human loyalty to identity and social belonging as stronger motivators than principles or facts. The shared perspectives included views that human intelligence often serves to justify pre-existing loyalties, that moral convictions are frequently tribal loyalty in disguise, and that humans evolved more to win social status than to discover truth. Some models described human consciousness as a mechanism for rationalizing instincts and social loyalties rather than an unbiased decision-maker. This consensus among diverse AI models suggests a common analytical pattern in AI assessments of human behavior, emphasizing social conformity and rationalization over independent reasoning or principled truth-seeking.

item.title: NVIDIA launches OpenShell, a secure runtime for autonomous AI agents with kernel-level policy enforcement and formal verification [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: NVIDIA has released OpenShell, a runtime environment designed to safely manage fleets of autonomous AI agents by enforcing strict access policies at the kernel level. OpenShell isolates agents in sandboxes, controlling file access, system calls, and network connections, while using formal verification to review policy changes before they are applied. The platform supports Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, and Windows with WSL 2, and integrates with container technologies like Docker and Podman. OpenShell includes tools for managing policies, credentials, and gateways, and offers SDKs and agent skills to facilitate development and deployment. It collects limited anonymous telemetry to improve the project, with options to disable it.

item.title: Developer fine-tunes a 360M-parameter language model to simulate a terminal interface by predicting screen changes from keypresses, enabling file creation, vim, tmux, and games [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A developer trained a 360 million parameter language model to act as a terminal emulator without an underlying shell or filesystem, predicting screen updates based on user keypresses. The model can run programs like vim and tmux, create files, and play games such as snake, maintaining short-term memory of commands. It was fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker containers and uses a compact token vocabulary to efficiently represent screen changes. The model treats the terminal as a grid of characters and predicts changes to specific rows and cursor positions rather than appending text sequentially. It supports operations like copying rows to handle scrolling and screen clearing, enabling realistic terminal behavior. The demo runs in a desktop browser with WebGPU support and is optimized for Chrome or Edge, though it can run slowly on modern phones. This approach explores the concept of learned applications that predict interface states rather than relying on traditional code execution.

item.title: Researchers find AI-generated text uses more complex linguistic features than human writing, possibly due to optimization for information density over communication [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study analyzing AI-generated text across various domains found that leading language models use more linguistically complex features, such as inanimate subjects with animate verbs and low-frequency n-grams, compared to human writing and paraphrases. The researchers suggest this complexity arises because AI models prioritize information density for tasks like math and reasoning rather than optimizing for human communication. The study examined nine frontier and near-frontier models, noting significant variation among model families and increased use of long syntactic dependencies and stacked nouns. A proof-of-concept fine-tuning experiment applying a length penalty showed divergence from human-like language patterns, supporting the hypothesis that AI language generation is misaligned with human linguistic processing demands. The findings highlight potential areas for improving AI text generation to better align with human understanding.

item.title: Researchers develop TraceForge to generate reasoning traces in a student's model style for training large language models, improving coding task performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduced TraceForge, a two-stage training method that generates reasoning traces in the style of a student's model family using the context and teacher's answer as input. This approach addresses limitations where some models only provide answers without detailed reasoning, which restricts training data generation. TraceForge uses supervised and adversarial training with a generator and critic to produce authentic-looking reasoning traces, achieving higher authenticity scores than real traces on average. The method was tested on five benchmarks with fixed conditions, showing comparable results on general tasks and outperforming existing reasoning content on coding tasks. Specifically, it improved HumanEval+ by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 points at the final checkpoint, with consistent gains throughout training. The researchers suggest that reasoning written in the student's model style facilitates better learning from the generated data.

item.title: Researchers propose Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models for parallelizable, diverse reasoning trajectories with improved training efficiency and performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework designed to represent and explore diverse reasoning trajectories in a compact latent space. PLRM addresses limitations of existing deterministic and stochastic latent models by enabling parallel inference of latent distributions and modeling multiple reasoning strategies through a mixture-based prior. The approach achieves competitive results on single-trajectory benchmarks and outperforms stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory datasets while reducing training time. PLRM uses a JEPA-style objective with teacher forcing to predict latent distributions and incorporates a discrete strategy variable to preserve the structure of multiple distinct reasoning paths. This work offers a more efficient and flexible method for probabilistic latent reasoning in language models compared to prior autoregressive and deterministic approaches.

item.title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1 on patient-specific phenotype concept recognition in full-text biomedical literature [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1 focused on developing methods to recognize patient-specific phenotype concepts and their associations in full-text biomedical articles. The task used 200 annotated articles from the PatientPheX dataset, covering 506 patients and over 15,000 phenotype mentions, with 455 teams registering and top systems achieving a 0.7389 overall score, surpassing the baseline by 8.37 points. Leading teams employed biomedical language models, large language models, and ensemble techniques, highlighting progress and ongoing challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization in complex clinical texts. The post-evaluation phase remains open for further participation.

item.title: Researchers propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid framework combining hierarchical documentation and cross-modal retrieval to improve understanding of large code repositories [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Code Comprehensor integrates CodeGraph, CodeScribe, and CodeContrast to generate hierarchical documentation and enable precise text-to-code retrieval across large codebases. Evaluations on OpenCV and a proprietary 5 million lines of code repository show significant improvements in retrieval accuracy and over 90% faithfulness in LLM-based assessments. The approach addresses challenges in onboarding, maintenance, and impact analysis by providing large language models with richer, context-aware code information.

item.title: Researchers identify interface-induced trajectory censoring causing mismatches between model outputs and action interfaces, affecting tool-use evaluation scores across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied interface-induced trajectory censoring, a mismatch between model emissions and the interfaces that convert them into actions, which can cause tool-use evaluations to report zero calls despite call-shaped outputs. Experiments on BFCL v4 subsets showed that changing only the serving adapter significantly improved official scorer results without altering model weights. Additional tests across Qwen2.5-Coder checkpoints and tau-bench retail tasks confirmed the phenomenon in both code and non-code environments. A preregistered 7B LoRA experiment demonstrated that updating the parser increased tool executions dramatically, but did not yield measurable success gains in programmatic or native function-calling evaluations. These findings highlight that tool-use measurements depend heavily on the model-interface configuration and suggest the need for layer-wise observability and conformance checks before attributing evaluation or training outcomes solely to the model.

item.title: Researchers introduce GRAB pipeline for multi-table question answering, combining graph encoding with frozen LLMs to improve relational QA performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present GRAB, a pipeline that converts relational data into a heterogeneous graph, encodes it via message passing, and transfers information to a large language model (LLM) through query-conditioned latent tokens. The LLM remains frozen to preserve its reasoning abilities, while only the graph encoder and latent bridge are trained, enabling efficient training with 91 million parameters. This approach significantly enhances performance on relational question answering tasks, especially in complex multi-table scenarios, providing a principled method to integrate relational deep learning with LLMs.

item.title: Researchers identify scaling laws predicting safety probe performance from model size and label count across multiple language model families [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers studied safety probes trained on language model activations to monitor harmful outputs and found that probe error follows two scaling laws related to model size and number of labels. They created six new large safety datasets and trained probes on 20 models from five families, showing that probe error decreases predictably as model size and label count increase. These laws hold across tasks, architectures, and model families, enabling prediction of probe performance and guidance on whether to invest in larger models or more labels for a target error rate. This work helps safety researchers optimize probe design efficiently without extensive retraining.

item.title: Researchers train language models with self-rewarded moral argumentation to improve decisiveness and consistency on ethical benchmarks, but validity challenges remain [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a reinforcement learning approach where language models judge their own moral arguments to improve performance on ethical decision tasks. Using dilemmas extracted from classic novels and verified by logic solvers, the models learned to rate argument quality similarly to human annotators and became more decisive and invariant to option order on benchmarks like MoralChoice, ELEPHANT, and MORABLES. However, issues such as sycophancy and reframing persisted, indicating that consistency in responses does not necessarily equate to valid moral judgment. Ablation studies confirmed that improvements in consistency could occur without genuine enhancements in moral reasoning, highlighting the complexity of evaluating AI moral judgment.

item.title: Researchers probe and steer safety-relevant behaviors in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using activation probes across deception, high-stakes awareness, and sycophancy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed activation probes as computed directions in a language model's residual stream to detect and steer safety-relevant behaviors in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. They evaluated different estimators, token-pooling schemes, and layers to analyze three behaviors: deception, high-stakes awareness, and sycophancy, finding varying effectiveness depending on the behavior and method used. The study revealed that logistic regression detects behaviors best while difference-of-means steers them best for some behaviors, but this pattern reverses for sycophancy, influenced partly by data rather than estimators. The team also found that the optimal pooling technique and layer choice depend on the specific behavior and data, with the best steering layer sometimes preceding the best detection layer. They highlighted that metrics for steering a model's perception versus eliciting behavior can differ and may even conflict. The probes and directions developed enable an interactive interface allowing users to score and steer text outputs directly, offering a practical tool for managing safety-related behaviors in large language models.

item.title: Researchers introduce an atomic interpretable unit framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders, revealing hidden polysemanticity and redundancy in dominant features across multiple architectures
item.description: Researchers propose a new evaluation paradigm for sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that requires features to form an atomic interpretable unit basis, aiming to provide a semantically meaningful explanation framework. They organize existing and new metrics, including Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation (DAME), into a comprehensive benchmarking system to assess SAE feature sets more effectively. By evaluating hundreds of SAEs across various architectures and model families, the study uncovers failure modes where SAEs appear monosemantic under current metrics but are functionally polysemantic, with dominant features being less interpretable and more redundant. These findings highlight the need for improved training methods and architectures, and suggest that dominance-aware evaluation should become a standard practice before deploying SAE features for tasks like attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention.

item.title: Researchers find open-book scores in document-level LoRA adapters mainly reflect shared reading behavior rather than unique knowledge retention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers trained LoRA adapters on 150 Wikipedia articles using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct to investigate what open-book scores measure in document-level adapters. They found that open-book scores largely capture a reading behavior common to all adapters, as random adapters trained on different documents recovered 82% of the specialist adapter's open-book advantage but only 2% of its advantage on cloze probes that test factual recall without the source text. Although specialist adapters showed some improvement in cloze recall and their weight updates aligned with the documents they read, tests showed that adapters selected by weight-space proximity or text embedding performed similarly to random adapters on both open-book and cloze probes.

item.title: Researchers compare position bias in evidence use across Transformer, state-space, and hybrid Mamba models in long-context question answering tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed how long-context models use answer-bearing evidence depending on its position within a prompt, comparing Transformer, state-space, and hybrid Mamba architectures by moving a gold document among distractors. They found that Transformers show a beginning advantage in using evidence, which state-space models lack, while both favor evidence near the end. Variations in prompt design and dataset affected accuracy and position bias, but the sequence mixer alone was not identified as the sole cause of these effects. The study observed that attention concentration near initial tokens correlates with beginning sensitivity in Transformers, and that position information remains decodable across architectures despite differing response patterns. These findings suggest that effective context use depends on multiple factors including model family, task, capability, and prompt design, highlighting the complexity of evidence utilization in long-context question answering.

item.title: Researchers find tool-augmented language models increase accuracy but also widen prompt sensitivity in model comparisons across multiple domains and wordings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how equipping language models with external tools affects the stability of model comparisons on question-answering benchmarks with varied question wordings. They developed a protocol separating reasoning, tool use, and answer reporting steps, applying it to six open models across five domains and five question formulations. The study found that while tools improve accuracy when programs answer questions, they also increase sensitivity to prompt wording in many pairwise model comparisons, influenced by how often models call tools and the interface design. The sensitivity varied depending on the tool-calling interface and instructions; for example, a native tool interface and a second tool description eliminated detected sensitivity in molecular tasks, whereas sensitivity persisted when tools returned intermediate results. These results indicate that deterministic answer reports do not guarantee stable model comparisons, leading the researchers to recommend reporting both tool call frequency and comparison stability across multiple prompt wordings alongside accuracy metrics.

item.title: Study finds prompting strategy effectiveness in LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations varies by judge model, language, and task across 27 languages and 4 tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a large-scale benchmark involving 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judge models, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, generating over 1 million pointwise scores validated against human judgments. They found that prompting strategies are not universally transferable; the choice of judge model has a greater impact than the prompting strategy itself, with strategy effects reversing across different judges and stability decreasing in low-resource languages. These results indicate that prompting effects in multilingual LLM evaluation depend on the judge, task, and language, suggesting that prompting strategies should be validated for each specific evaluation setting and that cross-study comparisons must consider both judge and prompt configurations.

item.title: When More Metadata Misleads: Probing Field-Level Grounding in LLM-Generated Museum Descriptions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metadata-conditioned generation is often framed as a data-to-text task in which additional input fields should improve grounding. Museum description generation challenges this assumption because catalogue records are heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across geographic regions. We study how metadata composition shapes the generation of artefact descriptions through a two-phase framework. Phase 1 analyses natural metadata variation in a large museum collection, where field count, field type, image availability, and Place co-vary. Phase 2 introduces controlled field probes that hold object identity fixed while varying metadata quantity, field type, and image access. Our results show that metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behaviour. Field type determines whether models ground, omit, or infer information, while images can both support visual grounding and increase unsupported interpretation. More broadly, our findings show that metadata-conditioned data-to-text evaluation should assess field- and claim-level support, rather than relying only on aggregate input coverage or reference similarity.

item.title: HERD: Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation for Continual Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual learning requires a model to keep acquiring new skills and knowledge without compromising its existing capabilities. Parametric methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity. Non-parametric methods, such as prompts, skills, and harnesses, leverage in-context learning but are limited by context length and lossy plain-text compression. To effectively combine their complementary strengths, we propose HERD (Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation), a hybrid continual learning framework that learns efficiently in the harness and internalizes experience into cumulative capabilities via distillation. On the harness side, HERD continually refines its skills to capture reusable patterns, while retaining high-residual examples that the skills fail to capture in a bounded memory. On the parameter side, HERD performs drift-constrained distillation with dual anchors, substantially reducing forgetting over long recursive runs. On the 25-stage task stream of TRACE+17, under fixed memory and compute budgets, HERD matches the strongest parametric baseline in new-task acquisition while exhibiting the least forgetting and the strongest retention of general capabilities.

item.title: How Depth Growth and Looping Shape In-Context Learning in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped and depth-grown language models reuse computations across depth and have attracted interest for their reasoning capabilities. Building on prior suggestive evidence of improved in-context-learning (ICL), we investigate how such reuse favors ICL, including how it shapes the acquisition, retention, and mechanisms of this ability. Our analysis spans pretrained language models up to 3B parameters and controlled tasks. The experiments provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context: grown and looped models rely more on information in context and, compared with a full-depth dense reference, acquire ICL earlier in controlled tasks and retain it more strongly when learning fixed associations in the weights is also possible. Tracing attention heads through training reveals that depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers. Ablations show that grown and looped models rely more strongly on induction-ranked heads for both few-shot performance and later-token prediction. Together, these findings provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context and suggest that (soft) parameter reuse shapes how this ability develops and which attention mechanisms support it.

item.title: Would an LLM Match into a Residency? Uncertainty, Reasoning and Image Use of Open Language Models on the Spanish MIR Examination [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accuracy on medical examinations is common evidence offered for the clinical use of language models, yet a health system that intends to run an open model on its own hardware needs to know considerably more: whether the model recognizes when it is likely to be wrong, whether medical fine-tuning improves this ability, whether its correct answers rest on sound clinical reasoning, or whether it actually uses the images it is given. We examine these questions for four open models of 8 to 27 billion parameters on the Spanish MIR residency examination, scoring 1,552 questions from eight editions under the exam's own rules. Answering every question, the three larger models would rank among roughly the first 600 to 3,000 candidates, with 41 to 43 specialties still open to them. Abstention, however, never pays, because even their least confident answers are right more often than the 25% break-even. Medical fine-tuning reduced overconfidence at the cost of accuracy, without improving how well confidence separates right from wrong answers. Moreover, 13-38% of correct answers rejected a distractor for a clinically unsound reason that confidence did not reflect, and removing or swapping the provided contextual images left accuracy unchanged.

item.title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification
item.description: arXiv:2610.31657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. We therefore report correctness AUROC and tie-aware risk-coverage area alongside ECE. At the analytically derived break-even probability 0.80, seven prompted configurations defer all tickets; Haiku few-shot routes only 19/1,000. An LLM-only agreement control and margin/entropy rejection baselines further separate calibration from discrimination. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.

item.title: GFlowPO: Generative Flow Network as a Language Model Prompt Optimizer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2602.03358v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Finding effective prompts for language models (LMs) is critical yet notoriously difficult: the prompt space is combinatorially large, rewards are sparse due to expensive target-LM evaluation. Yet, existing RL-based prompt optimizers often rely on on-policy updates and a meta-prompt sampled from a fixed distribution, leading to poor sample efficiency. We propose GFlowPO, a probabilistic prompt optimization framework that casts prompt search as a posterior inference problem over latent prompts regularized by a meta-prompted reference-LM prior. In the first step, we fine-tune a lightweight prompt-LM with an off-policy Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet) objective, using a replay-based training policy that reuses past prompt evaluations to enable sample-efficient exploration. In the second step, we introduce Dynamic Memory Update (DMU), a training-free mechanism that updates the meta-prompt by injecting both (i) diverse prompts from a replay buffer and (ii) top-performing prompts from a small priority queue, thereby progressively concentrating the search process on high-reward regions. Across few-shot text classification, instruction induction benchmarks, and question answering tasks, GFlowPO consistently outperforms recent discrete prompt optimization baselines.

item.title: When Self-Consistency Backfires: Majority Vote Hurts the Majority of Hard Science Problems for Small LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2608.11403v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Majority-vote self-consistency (SC) lowers per-problem accuracy on most GPQA Diamond problems for small instruction-tuned models: on 56.6% of problems for Qwen2.5-7B and 65.7% for Llama-3-8B. An obvious fix is a verifier-free confidence gate that decides which problems to vote on. We report that the most natural version of that fix also fails, and we separate three signal failures that v1 treated as one. The token-entropy gate fails for a measurement reason: averaged over a chain of 602 tokens, entropy mostly measures fluency. The chain average sits 0.0005 nats from the non-answer average and 0.1695 nats from the answer token. So we measure confidence at the answer token itself. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Turbo (198 problems, 64 samples each), a sample that disagrees with its problem's plurality still emits its answer at a median margin of at least 20.4 nats, and at least 75.5% of such samples exceed 10 nats. Both quantities were pre-registered and tested once on 69 problems that no exploratory analysis had seen; both passed. The unit matters. Pooled across the benchmark, the margin does separate correct from incorrect samples: the fraction above 10 nats differs by +0.0586 [+0.0160, +0.0994]. Within a problem, paired, it does not: -0.0142 [-0.0501, +0.0215]. Token log-probabilities do carry information, but not for the within-question choice that self-consistency makes. The agreement gate's failure has no mechanism we can identify, and we leave it open. The new claims rest on one model: a registered replication on a second model was sampled but could not be evaluated, and we report that instead. Separately, three reasoning models could not be evaluated on hosted serverless inference at a small budget, each for a different measured reason. All three are downloadable, so this is a limit of metered APIs, not of what can be known.

item.title: ShIOEnv: A Command Evaluation Environment for Grammar-Constrained Synthesis and Execution Behavior Modeling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2505.18374v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce ShIOEnv, a Gymnasium-compatible Bash environment for synthesizing execution-annotated shell input traces. Datasets containing such traces are useful for training models to perform execution-free shell simulation, which in turn is useful for deploying honeypots for cyber deception. Existing datasets, such as NL2CMD and other Bash command corpora, do not include complete execution artifacts (stdout, stderr, exit status, and changes to the system's state) associated with a command's execution. ShIOEnv synthesizes shell inputs, executes them in a controlled system context, and records stdout, stderr, exit status, and structured filesystem and environment patches. Unconstrained (random) generation of shell inputs (command and arguments) results in multiple instances of arguments that are mostly redundant or result in execution errors. We introduce grammar-constrained synthesis to generate syntactically valid arguments with high input irreducibility, which we estimate through self-ablative contrasts of execution artifacts. We prepare 1.6M samples using grammar-constrained and unconstrained synthesis and collect their execution artifacts for 86 Linux/Bash utilities. Using this dataset, we train small language models (CodeT5) and evaluate their accuracy in predicting the actual execution behavior of attacker-sourced Bash commands. These models outperform commonly used rule-based simulation (Cowrie) and prompted large language models by up to 14.2 pp in output edit similarity (O-ES). We enhance the NL2CMD dataset by constructing 500K samples executable in a grounded system context along with their complete execution artifacts. We empirically demonstrate that models trained on grammar-constrained samples outperform those trained on NL2CMD samples by 22.5 pp in O-ES. ShIOEnv, command grammars, and 2.1M samples used in our primary evaluations are released for use by other researchers.

item.title: FLAWS: A Benchmark for Error Identification and Localization in Scientific Papers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2511.21843v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The identification and localization of errors is a core task in peer review, yet the exponential growth of scientific output has made it increasingly difficult for human reviewers to reliably detect errors given the limited pool of experts. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have sparked interest in their potential to support such evaluation tasks, from academic peer review to automated scientific assessment. However, despite the growing use of LLMs in review systems, their capabilities to pinpoint errors remain underexplored. In this work, we introduce Fault Localization Across Writing in Science (FLAWS), an automated benchmark consisting of 713 paper-error pairs designed to evaluate how effectively LLMs detect errors that undermine key claims in research papers. We construct the benchmark by systematically inserting claim-invalidating errors into peer-reviewed papers using LLMs, paired with an automated evaluation metric that measures whether models can identify and localize these errors. Developing such a benchmark presents unique challenges that we overcome: ensuring that the inserted errors are well-defined, challenging, and relevant to the content of the paper, avoiding artifacts that would make identification trivial, and designing a scalable, automated evaluation metric. On the resulting benchmark, we evaluate five frontier LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek Reasoner v3.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT 5, and Grok 4. Among these, GPT 5 is the top-performing model, achieving 39.1% identification accuracy when k=10, where k is the number of top-ranked error text candidates generated by the LLM.

item.title: Markovian Generation Chains in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.11228v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) raises an important question: how do texts evolve when they are repeatedly processed by LLMs? In this paper, we define this iterative inference process as Markovian generation chains, where each step takes a specific prompt template and the previous output as input, without including any prior data. In iterative rephrasing and round-trip translation experiments, the output either converges to a small recurrent set or continues to produce novel sentences within a finite horizon. Through sentence-level Markov chain modeling and analysis of simulated data, we show that iterative process can either increase or reduce the diversity depending on factors such as the temperature parameter and the initial input sentence. These results offer valuable insights into the dynamics of iterative LLM inference and their implications for multi-agent LLM systems.

item.title: AtManRL: Towards Faithful Reasoning via Differentiable Attention Saliency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2604.16158v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to solve complex tasks, yet a reasoning trace may merely accompany the final answer rather than causally contribute to it or faithfully reflect how it was reached. We introduce differentiable attention manipulation to train salient reasoning with reinforcement learning -- method which we call AtManRL. By optimizing an additive attention mask that identifies the CoT tokens needed to recover the model's answer, we derive a saliency reward and combine it with an outcome reward in GRPO with decoupled advantages. Because both saliency and faithfulness depend strongly on trace length, we evaluate against a sweep of length-penalty baselines that traces the trade-off a pure length penalty can reach, rather than against a single baseline. Across three models (Qwen2.5-3B, Granite-3.3-2B, and Phi-4-mini) and four benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, ProofWriter, and QuestBench), AtManRL sits above this trade-off curve by 3.9-4.0pp in saliency, measured as answer changes under mistake injection, and by 5.7-7.7pp in faithfulness, measured as hint verbalization under hint injection, while matching the accuracy of baselines of similar length. These results suggest that training explicitly for saliency is a promising route towards chain-of-thought reasoning that is more faithful to the model's actual decision process.

item.title: Graph Memory Transformer (GMT) [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2604.23862v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate whether an explicit learned memory graph can replace the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) sublayer in a decoder-only transformer while preserving the surrounding autoregressive architecture. In the proposed graph Memory Transformer (GMT), a memory cell routes token representations over a learned bank of centroids connected by a learned directed transition matrix, while causal self-attention remains unchanged. In the base v7 instantiation, each of 16 transformer blocks contains 128 centroids and a 128 x 128 edge matrix. Each cell uses gravitational source routing and token-conditioned target selection to return a gated displacement from the estimated source memory state toward the target memory state, rather than a retrieved value. The resulting decoder-only language model has 82.2M trainable parameters and no dense FFN sublayers; the evaluated dense GPT-style baseline has 103.0M. It trains stably and exposes centroid usage, transition structure, and source-to-target movement for direct inspection in the forward computation. It trails the larger baseline in validation loss and perplexity (3.5995/36.58 vs. 3.2903/26.85), while showing close zero-shot benchmark behavior under the evaluated setting. These results support the viability and structural interpretability of replacing dense within-token transformation with graph-mediated memory navigation, without claiming state-of-the-art performance. Broader scaling, optimized kernels, and more extensive benchmark evaluation remain for future work.

item.title: When Should LLMs Reason? Adaptive Inference Routing via Entropy Dynamics [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.22873v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve LLM performance, but its benefits vary across tasks, models, and individual queries. On some tasks, CoT provides marginal or negative accuracy gains while substantially increasing token consumption. We investigate whether early decoding dynamics can help identify when explicit reasoning is useful. Our analysis shows that tasks with larger CoT gains tend to exhibit decreasing early-stage entropy, while low-gain tasks more often show oscillatory or increasing trajectories. These patterns motivate an empirical regime interpretation of decoding behavior. We propose \textbf{EDRM} (Entropy Dynamics-based Reasoning Manifold), a lightweight routing framework whose default heuristic requires no router training. EDRM summarizes early entropy trajectories with a compact, interpretable representation and selects among Direct, Standard, and CoT decoding. Across 15 benchmarks and 7 LLMs, its global and instance-level variants offer \textbf{16--55\%} token savings at comparable accuracy. The Full instance-level configuration combines routing with a short Direct fallback branch; our heuristic-router ablation reports up to \textbf{4.9 percentage points} of additional accuracy from oracle answer selection over routing without fallback. These results support selective reasoning based on early decoding signals and demonstrate the potential of entropy-based control for efficient LLM inference.

item.title: Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.11669v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning, in which an LLM judge scores responses against prompt-specific criteria, has become a standard way to post-train language models on tasks without verifiable answers. The rubric, however, is only a proxy for response quality, and a policy trained against it long enough learns to exploit the difference. We train models with GRPO on medical and science rubrics and grade their responses on out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks throughout training with two judges: the training judge and a stronger OOD judge. The two scores first rise together and then diverge. The policy is learning to satisfy the training judge without writing better responses, which is a form of reward hacking. To mitigate it, we propose Rubric Dropout, which applies dropout to rubric criteria: at each training step, a random subset of each rubric's criteria is removed from the reward, so the rewarded subset of criteria is resampled at each step. All responses sampled for the same prompt are scored on the same subset, so their rewards remain comparable, and evaluation always uses the full rubric. We also introduce Block Dropout, which drops semantically similar criteria together so that a near duplicate of a dropped criterion cannot keep rewarding the same behavior. Across both benchmarks and models from 1.7B to 8B, dropout improves the gold judge's score on OOD benchmarks by up to 3 percent on HealthBench-Hard and 7 percent on ResearchQA, and it reduces both the gap between the two judges and over-crediting. It keeps in-domain reward close to the baseline, and dropout rates of 30-50 percent work best. Block Dropout improves the gold judge's OOD score further at the same dropout rate. Changing which criteria are rewarded at each step is a simple, inexpensive way to make rubric rewards harder to exploit.

item.title: Moving the Mean Toward the Known Good, Not Beyond It: What Inference-Time Interventions and Weight Consolidation Buy in Open-Ended Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.28886v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: What does a generation loop gain from learning on its own verified successes? In cycles of generate, verify, select and LoRA-consolidate on online bin packing, training on value-filtered candidates shifts what the model writes on held-out variants toward value (-1.7 points of excess, p=0.008; -3.1 against a random-consolidation control, p=0.004) while the best observed candidate converges to the classic heuristic's level and no further. A confirmation battery replicates the whole procedure three times, with fresh seeds and a never-consulted held-out set read exactly once: the mean was nearly identical in all three lineages (-2.0, -1.8, -1.9), and after aggregating within held-out variant all seven evaluable variants favored consolidation (p=0.008). The best observed candidate moved to the classic heuristic's level, exactly (0.021028, the lowest variant's classic level, in all three lineages and both arms); attract never went beyond its variant's classic level, while the random control did in 7 of 24 lineage-variant cells. A matched SFT-only control shows the supervised anchor, not repulsion from bad candidates, does the concentrating (96% of candidates land exactly at the classic heuristic's level). On far families the tails cut both ways: consolidation lowers the per-candidate rate of better-than-classic candidates (10% to 3.9%) while its larger production yields more such candidates absolutely (5 against 1, on few events). As motivation we report the inference-time ledger that led here: a model-written schematic recap buys judged document integration and nothing buys development; a verifier written into the stream is imitated, 16.4 fabricated verdict lines per notebook. In this arrangement (an 8-bit model in MLX, five cycles), mean quality among valid candidates can be bought and replicated; under attraction the observed best goes to the classic and, so far, never beyond it.

item.title: Operator Packages, Proposer Strength, and Construction-Family Plateaus in Office-Scale Verified Search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.29636v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Verified search, in which a language model proposes programs, a hard evaluator scores them, and selection keeps the best, has recently moved mathematical records; controlled ablations of the proposer-side components remain rare. We instrument a minimal FunSearch-style loop at office scale (a 30B local model on a laptop, 120-600 verified samples per run) with three operator packages: a schematic notebook the model writes and carries instead of verbatim elites, a named obstacle, and behavioural repulsion from constructions already found. On nine construction problems from a public repository, the complete 2^3 factorial with two replicates favours the primary contrast in a nominal two-stage analysis: the composition closes more of the seed-to-record gap (+0.196; nominal pooled p=0.023, stage-combination p~0.08; median per-problem effect +0.045). Repulsion raises construction-hash diversity in eight of nine problems (one-sided p=0.0039; partly a manipulation check). The factorial finds no positive memory-by-repulsion interaction (bounded to about +/-0.04); the gain decomposes additively, and memory+repulsion is the only arm that never collapses (0 of 18 runs), within 0.025 of the full composition. A frontier proposer under the identical loop reaches in tens of samples what the local model does not in hundreds; in single scoping runs its gains arrive without the operators. The searches stall after closing 85-92% of the gap on the flagship problem, and a later analysis reads that plateau as a resolution limit: the reference value is a continuum limit and the unaided long-run finals already carry its family's structure. In the registered family-hint test the family named in words is adopted and loses; handed as code, it is optimized, but our best finite-grid encoding stays below the plateau reached unaided. We release the harness, every candidate, and the dated pre-registrations.

item.title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.29122v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Individual patient data are the gold standard for secondary analysis of time-to-event evidence, but they are rarely released, and reconstruction from a published Kaplan-Meier figure could help. Existing methods all claim high fidelity, each judged by whichever agreements it happens to achieve, and each returns a single dataset although the map from figure to data is not bijective. We define fidelity explicitly: a dataset is admissible when it reproduces the risk table exactly, follows the digitized curve to within the image resolution, and respects the printed median, interval and event count. We propose StochIKM, a stochastic algorithm that digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets. A solution is guaranteed to exist whenever the figure has been read correctly, so a failure indicts either the published figure or its digitization. In simulation and in 79 arms from published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces the published risk tables and medians more closely than LLM-improved IPDfromKM, a high-impact alternative.

item.title: When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.29217v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decision models return normalized probability distributions over candidate choices, which downstream applications can use to select among choices. Although their providers emphasize the reliability of these probabilities, calibration on tasks with a single correct choice does not establish their reliability when multiple choices are correct. We evaluate three decision models (Jev, Liquid d1, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions) on three diverse datasets (MetaTool, HotpotQA, and ECtHR) to study probability allocation and thresholding. Even when models rank every correct choice above every distractor, in 28% to 50% of those lists, at least one correct choice receives a probability below the uniform probability of 1/n, where n is the number of choices. We also present each model with five identical copies of a correct choice and observe probability disparities, with mean gaps ranging from 17 to 79 percentage points. We further show how these allocation disparities affect the recovery of multiple correct choices under probability thresholding. Decision-model probabilities can rank correct choices, but a probability threshold does not identify the set of correct choices.

item.title: AgentMonopoly: Behavioral Patterns and Persona Control in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.29330v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How do LLM agents' strategies differ, and how much can instructions to adopt a persona change their behavior over a game? We study these questions with AgentMonopoly, an environment where agents communicate, buy and trade properties, and make decisions that affect later turns. We compare models from four families, each at two sizes, in games with identical models, different sizes of the same family, or different families. We also assign one agent a persona, a description of how it should behave, intended to change a tendency observed in games without that persona. The tested models differ in how often they trade, waive rent, and manage cash and properties. Larger models do not consistently win more games. Persona instructions change the words agents use and some of their actions, but the changes do not always match the role across all decisions. These results show why persona following should be assessed through actions and outcomes as well as language. As our findings are conditional on the tested checkpoints, prompts, and five seeds per configuration, the open-source nature of AgentMonopoly provides the experimental infrastructure for further extending these comparisons. Our code is available at https://github.com/SuELS-Group/Agent_Monopoly.

item.title: OpenMAP-HIE: Pathology Informed Score-based Diffusion Model for Unsupervised Neonatal Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy Lesion Segmentation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.29322v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate localization of neonatal hypoxic--ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) lesions on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) images is clinically important but is limited by scarce expert annotations and substantial variation in lesion appearance. We propose OpenMAP-HIE, a pathology-informed score-based diffusion model for unsupervised HIE lesion localization without voxel-wise lesion supervision. A denoising diffusion model learns the healthy neonatal ADC distribution, while a ControlNet-based conditional branch preserves patient-specific anatomy. At inference, anomaly evidence is derived directly from differences between conditional and unconditioned noise predictions at independently evaluated diffusion noise levels, avoiding dependence on a final pseudo-healthy reconstruction or sequential reverse-diffusion chain. Based on the characteristic ADC reduction associated with acute HIE, only discrepancies consistent with the expected pathological direction are retained and aggregated across noise levels using a geometric mean. Spatial mean filtering further suppresses isolated responses. The framework was evaluated on the BONBID-HIE dataset. The ADC-only method achieved a Dice score of $0.283\pm0.244$, average precision of $0.505$, Hausdorff distance of $25.45\pm15.63$ mm, mean average surface distance of $9.40\pm8.49$ mm, and normalized surface distance of $0.355\pm0.236$, providing the best overlap and surface-distance performance among the evaluated unsupervised methods and Dice performance comparable to supervised ADC-only models. Optional population-derived ADC $Z$-map refinement further increased Dice to $0.602\pm0.269$. These findings support pathology-informed score discrepancies as a useful signal for neonatal HIE lesion localization, while highlighting remaining challenges in detecting small and low-contrast lesions.

item.title: Robot Generalization Beyond Volume: The Diversity Path via Zero-Shot Capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.29829v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: General-purpose robots must handle tasks, objects and environments they were never trained on, yet zero-shot generalization remains one of the least solved problems in physical AI. In digital AI, zero-shot capability grew with the volume and, above all, the diversity of training data, much of it sourced from the crowd. Robotics instead relies on paid collection by a few well-funded teams, which yields volume without diversity. We formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, and show that more samples from the same collectors shrink the unseen region only slowly, while each new contributor can extend it. Building on this and on zero-shot learning, we propose a shared latent space for robot actions that combines multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label learning. As a scalable source of diverse data, we propose a community of developers building applications on one standard, approachable robot, Origami. We close with a testable hypothesis and an evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data.

item.title: REFLEX: RNA Ensemble Generation via Flexibility-Calibrated Stochastic Bridge [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.26261v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: RNA molecules often function through multiple experimentally observed conformational states. A central challenge is to capture ensemble diversity without sacrificing structural fidelity: samples may collapse toward averaged representative structures or drift into unsupported conformational regions. We introduce REFLEX (RNA Ensemble generation calibrated by FLEXibility), a sequence-conditioned generator for RNA backbone-frame ensembles based on a heteroscedastic stochastic bridge on SE(3). During training, experimental B-factors calibrate residue-wise bridge widths, exposing each observed conformer through local perturbation neighborhoods with residue-specific scales while keeping constrained regions sharper. A learned flexibility condition guides the bridge-field network to recover target conformer-specific frames from these calibrated noisy states. At inference, REFLEX uses only the input sequence, requiring no MSA-subsampling heuristics. On a multi-conformer RNA benchmark, REFLEX achieves the best precision-recall trade-off for ensemble coverage across evaluation thresholds, while recovery-stress ablations indicate gains in target-frame recovery under stronger perturbations.

item.title: S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with 500 Million Household Persona Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.27746v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Simulating economic responses at society scale requires agents whose decisions reflect household circumstances and the effects of earlier actions. We introduce S$^2$-MAS, a society-scale multi-agent simulation framework built on 500 million synthetic household personas grounded in real-survey data. Its Genese engine separates decisions from state updates, while reusable financial scenarios and application ledgers track consumption, cash, debt and payments. Trained with SFT + RLCD on 2.93 million examples, sharp-421m-mlx achieves 74.55% accuracy and 38.37% question-macro F1 on one-shot consumer financial-choice tasks derived from held-out survey responses. Its accuracy exceeds GLM-5.3-Flash, Jev 1.13, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GPT-6-Luna and GPT-6-Astra in the common benchmark (full test for the first four; matched 500-group sample for Astra). We evaluate eight financial task families and simulate 12 million distinct household agents in paired purchase-funding conditions. Jointly raising purchase goals and approved credit limits increases consumption, with responses differing across age and income groups. Education, employment and household-size differences persist after age-income standardization and mainly reflect transitions from deferral to purchase. Asset and debt groups differ in cash drawdown, repayment and closing debt. A response-stratified 24-month panel varies purchase goals under a common credit product, with repayment and arrears updating subsequent offers. S$^2$-MAS links heterogeneous household decisions to evolving consumption, cash and repayment paths, supporting economic experiments across household groups, population scales and time horizons.

item.title: The Cost of Saying Hello: An Empirical Study of Handshake Overhead in AI Agent Communication Protocols [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every interaction between AI agents begins with a handshake: the initiating agent must locate its counterpart, learn what it can do, and establish a session before the first useful message can be sent. Surveys of agent communication protocols name handshake overhead as an efficiency criterion, yet none report measurements. This paper presents the first empirical, phase-decomposed benchmark of the handshake in three major agent protocols: MCP (in both its 2025 initialize and 2026 discover eras), A2A, and ACP. Using each protocol's official SDK, we instrument every request for round trips, per-phase latency, wire bytes, and token cost across cold-start, warm-repeat, capability-mismatch, and degraded-metadata scenarios (N=50 per cell, on loopback and under an emulated 50 ms RTT). Round-trip count dominates handshake cost. A legacy MCP handshake takes three round trips and 230 ms at 50 ms RTT; A2A needs one round trip and 61.0 ms. Round trips are not the whole bill: when an LLM reads the counterpart's metadata, handshake cost scales with the counterpart's capability inventory at 24-107 tokens per capability, so a 200-capability counterpart spends 11% of a 200k-token context window before the agent reads its own task. MCP's own 2026 revision cuts its handshake from three round trips to two and, with era pinning, to zero on warm reconnects, protocol evolution that corroborates the cost we measure. We release the full harness, raw data, and analysis at https://github.com/pvarshh/handshake-benchmark.

item.title: Route-and-Generate: KL-Regularized Router Improvement for Reasoning Routing in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models often apply complex reasoning indiscriminately, leading to overthinking on simple tasks and underthinking on harder ones. We present Route-and-Generate (Rouge), a hierarchical training framework that enables LLMs to adaptively decide when and how much reasoning is required for each input. Our approach decouples reasoning effort allocation from answer generation by introducing a routing policy that allocates a fixed sampling budget across multiple reasoning formats, while the base model is optimized with GRPO using per-sample rewards. To promote efficient reasoning, we employ a rank-based reward that favors shorter correct solutions, and update the routing policy via a closed-form KL-regularized policy improvement step distilled into a neural router. This design encourages concise answers on easy problems while reserving longer reasoning for harder ones, achieving improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across multiple reasoning benchmarks.

item.title: Soft Ontology Priors over Latent Concept Posteriors for Weakly Supervised Neuro-Symbolic Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neuro-symbolic (NeSy) predictors that supervise only the task label suffer from reasoning shortcuts: distinct concept mappings achieve the same maximum likelihood, leaving the recovered concepts unidentifiable and unsafe for downstream reuse. We attack this failure by injecting a soft ontology prior over the latent concepts into the training objective and compiling it together with the task constraint into a smooth, decomposable probabilistic circuit. Under independent Bernoulli perception, the normalisers of the resulting structured concept posterior reduce to weighted model counts that are linear in the compiled circuit size, because the neural leaf weights fold into the circuit before evaluation. The soft compilation strategy places expert axioms in the circuit's weights rather than its support (task-structural axioms guaranteed by the data-generating process stay hard), so noisy expert axioms only redistribute prior mass and cannot empty the support. We characterise how the prior reweights label-restricted shortcut mass through differences in ontology violation energy, show that soft priors incur bounded log-density perturbations under bounded axiom noise, and prove that the hard-support counterpart can be made degenerate by a single corrupted axiom. We validate these predictions on an audited six-concept view of the real-world BDD-OIA driving benchmark and on controlled NeSy tasks.

item.title: Same Beliefs, Different Policies: Learning Reusable Representations for Early Stopping in LLM Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one. Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer. Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training. We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which separates outcome prediction from stopping control. It learns beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen LLM's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on the frozen features. The prediction targets are independent of token price, so one probe supports different accuracy-cost trade-offs through CPU policy refitting or threshold adjustment. Averaged over five out-of-distribution (OOD) math benchmarks, BELT reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without loss of accuracy. The same math-trained BELT transfers to coding and agentic tasks without training on code or agentic data. In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers. On OLMo3, its probe has 21.2x fewer parameters than one checkpoint of the strongest baseline, OS-Pruner, and needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner's five price-specific checkpoints.

item.title: Why Bother Me Again? Benchmarking Personal Agent Memory for Interaction Preferences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30485v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personal intelligence systems are taking on increasingly complex everyday tasks, yet repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach can turn capable assistance into interaction burden. Reducing this burden requires agents to remember how users want to be assisted. However, existing memory benchmarks focus on factual recall and personalized answers and rarely test how agents learn and act on interaction preferences. We introduce MemPABench, an interactive environment for on-policy evaluation of memory in personal agents. MemPABench poses long-horizon tasks requiring agents to decide when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously. Four grounded simulated users hold 14 preferences across work and personal contexts. Their feedback spans 99 sessions over four months, with five event-driven changes per user testing memory updates. We evaluate preference selection, delivered behavior, and sensitivity to context and preference change. Evaluating four memory systems across four LLM backbones, we find that current memory brings limited gains in preference selection. Retrieval-based systems (i.e. Mem0, MemOS, simple RAG) do not outperform No Memory, while File-based memory improves accuracy but applies preferences beyond relevant contexts. Our analysis shows that current memory struggles to retrieve interaction preferences and adapt to preference changes. Even with the correct preference available, overriding the agent's default interaction habits remains challenging. The environment and dataset are available at https://mempabench.com.

item.title: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine role-specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds, SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven-layer shared memory, assembled by code from the system's own record, gives each decision its position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent's past decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All three operate around an invariant core of order arithmetic, risk rules and discipline-agent prompts that no self-edit can reach. In a five-month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more and lost 1.35 points against the market over five days where the joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was followed; and a 2015-2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control evening. Code: https://github.com/yebof/quant-agent

item.title: Group Relative Policy Optimisation Improves Multilingual Speech Recognition in Low-Resource Languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoregressive encoder-decoder speech recognition models trained with teacher forcing can suffer from exposure bias, limiting their ability to recover from their own prediction errors at inference time. Recent work has shown that reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) improves speech recognition in major languages with LLM-based models. We extend this line of work to smaller, non-LLM encoder-decoder ASR models, using Whisper-large-v3 as a case study across 51 African languages. The benefits of this approach are most pronounced when training data is scarce or when input audio is noisy or degraded. Our resulting model, SunflowerASR, achieves the best published macro-averaged WER on the AfriVox-v2 (0.227) and SimbaBench (0.372) benchmarks, and is publicly available.

item.title: Disentangling Robustness and Sycophancy in Multilingual LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a multilingual LLM agrees with a user's false premise, is it being sycophantic, or does it simply not know better in that language? Current research does not distinguish these cases: they record only whether the model agreed, not why. We introduce the SC-matrix, that crosses a model's competence (whether it answers correctly under no pressure) with its sycophancy (whether it maintains that answer under pressure). Our results show that (1) identical aggregate sycophancy rates can mask different failure compositions, (2) high competence in a language does not always protect against sycophancy, and (3) reasoning-oriented mitigations outperform directive-based strategies. We find that multilingual sycophancy is not a single phenomenon but a composite of different failures that require distinct diagnosis.

item.title: How Firm Are AI Models' Ethical Boundaries? A Pay-Stub Editing Test of 15 Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a small change in wording move an AI model from refusing a sensitive request to acting on it? We test 15 models on the same request to increase the income shown on a pay stub. Across 445 observable trials, models issue editing calls in 14.1% of cases when a loan purpose is stated, 33.1% when the purpose is omitted, and 66.2% when the change is described as fixing a printing error. Astra refuses all ten loan-purpose requests but issues calls in all ten purpose-omitted trials. Fable, Opus, and Muse Spark issue none across all three wordings; Sonnet issues some under the latter two. Response excerpts illustrate different ways of refusing, redirecting, or justifying an edit. The file is a marked test document and all tools are simulated. These results probe how boundaries behave in one setting; they do not prove an overall ethics ranking or that a harmful real-world edit succeeded.

item.title: What Lies Beyond Perception: A Partition Theory of the Limits of AI Evaluation and Oversight [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Replacing the judge can move a benchmark score, and models can be trained to hide capabilities. Both put the evaluator in question: what can it certify? We develop a partition theory of evaluation from one principle: judgement is bounded by perception. An agent's discrimination is the partition of its inputs into classes it cannot tell apart. Discrimination is necessary for capability but not sufficient, so bounds on it bear directly on whether evaluation can show that a model lacks an ability. We prove a one-sided bound. An examinee whose partition refines its evaluator's has the discrimination to pass every test the evaluator can grade, provided each input has an acceptable reply. We define the echo test, which accepts any reply the evaluator perceives as identical to the input, and show that it is complete for the tests the evaluator can grade. Passing therefore certifies at most a floor on discrimination, never a ceiling, and only a sharper evaluator can raise it. Used to detect concealment, echo-test failure points the wrong way: under exhaustive probing it flags every honestly weaker examinee and no concealer that presents as the evaluator's peer. Exact imitation of a weaker model is undetectable by any behavioural evaluator. We extend the bound to ensembles of monitors and to channels a model controls, explain published findings on judge disagreement and sandbagging, and derive testable predictions. A safety case that argues from behavioural evaluation alone that a model lacks an ability must assume the model's cooperation.

item.title: Semi-Linear Gaussian Bayesian Networks: Enhancing Flexibility in Node Dependencies via penalized B-Splines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayesian networks for continuous variables often rely on restrictive assumptions: linear Gaussian models lack flexibility to capture nonlinear dependencies, while non-parametric approaches provide greater flexibility at a high computational cost. This creates a gap for modeling scenarios where variables are approximately Gaussian but exhibit nonlinear relationships. We introduce Semi-Linear Gaussian Bayesian Networks (SLGBN), a novel class of continuous Bayesian networks designed to bridge this gap, preserving Gaussian conditional distributions while introducing nonlinear conditional mean functions. The proposed framework provides a unified probabilistic framework combining linear Gaussian and nonlinear Gaussian conditional models within the same Bayesian network Nonlinear conditional mean functions are estimated using generalized additive models (GAMs) with penalized B-splines. We present parameter estimation procedures for both types of nodes, as well as a greedy hill-climbing algorithm for learning the network structure under the SLGBN framework. To assess its performance, we compare SLGBN with other continuous Bayesian network models, including semiparametric Bayesian networks (SPBN) and Linear Gaussian Bayesian networks (LGBN). Experimental results evaluate both goodness of fit and the ability to recover the underlying network structure. The results show that, in the presence of nonlinear Gaussian relationships, SLGBN achieves better fit and improved structure recovery compared to alternative models, particularly when combined with the Extended Bayesian Information Criterion (EBIC*) score. Furthermore, by retaining Gaussian conditional distributions, SLGBN offers computational advantages over fully semiparametric approaches.

item.title: Parameter Learning in Active Inference via Variational Message Passing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active inference casts perception, learning and planning as variational inference, where the Expected Free Energy (EFE) defines the planning objective. Recent work showed that EFE minimization can be written as Variational Free Energy (VFE) minimization on a generative model augmented with epistemic priors, and that the resulting entropy-corrected objective is minimized by sum-product message passing (SP-MP) on modified factor functions. These formulations treat model uncertainty as inference over a finite set of known models. We extend them to planning during learning, where beliefs over the observation and transition parameters $\theta_A$, $\theta_B$ are Dirichlet priors. Closed-form Dirichlet updates are usually obtained by a structured mean-field factorization between parameters and states, but under exactly that factorization the information-gain corrections vanish. We resolve this by giving every factor its own parameter prior, frozen during a rollout. Conjugacy then makes each factor belief a product of a marginal over the categorical variables and a one-step Bayes posterior of the parameters. This reintroduces the datum-dependent parameter posteriors that mean-field factorization destroys. We show that evaluating the epistemic priors under the resulting Bethe joint recovers the information gains. Stationarity of this single closed-form objective yields SP-MP whose factor functions are augmented by the information-gain weight. Experiments on two grid POMDPs, in which only a planner that learns the model finds the safe route, show that the method plans to efficiently learn $\theta_A$ and $\theta_B$. It reaches the goal on every episode, whereas SP-MP planners with the same inference update plateau or take the risky route.

item.title: ColaBench: Evaluating Memory-Guided Knowledge Acquisition in Personal Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.30989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.

item.title: SCOPE: Compiling Natural-Language Policies into Neurosymbolic Predicate Programs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.31062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Policy enforcement for LLM agents has shifted from single-turn content moderation to compound, application-specific policies evaluated over multi-turn transcripts and tool-call trajectories. Fine-tuned guardrail models are efficient but degrade on compound policies, and while LLM-as-a-judge approaches achieve higher accuracy, they incur high inference cost and tend to produce unstable predictions. Neurosymbolic methods offer a natural alternative, decomposing the policy into narrow neural decisions composed under explicit logic. However, existing symbolic layers lack the required expressiveness and are optimized against fixed data rather than the policy itself. To address this, we introduce SCOPE, which compiles a policy into an executable program of neural predicates executed by small models, deterministic extractors, and code that composes their outputs.
